overal.goal: bin/src/runner-guard.ts (the single-runner pidfile, `.runner.pid`) is a fifth pid lock that the process-lock work did not touch. It holds the pid alone, with no boot id, so after a crash and a reboot that reuses the pid `isHeld()` reports a live runner and the runner never starts; and `acquire()` is `isHeld()` followed by `writeFile`, which is not atomic, so two processes starting together can both believe they hold it. Make it a proper lock: either `withProcessLock`-style exclusive creation with the boot id (packages/shared/src/process-lock.ts), or reuse the identity of packages/runner/src/pid-file.ts (`bootId` plus `startTicks`, field 22 of /proc/<pid>/stat, which also detects pid reuse inside one boot). Keep reading old pid-only files, and keep the guard held for the whole life of the runner (it is not a short critical section like the task lock, so it needs its own acquire/release shape rather than a callback).

rules.do: Read bin/src/runner-guard.ts, packages/runner/src/pid-file.ts, packages/shared/src/process-lock.ts and where the guard is used (serve, run, the desktop app, the systemd unit) before changing code.

Write a failing test first: two processes acquiring at once (child processes) must yield exactly one holder; a guard file naming a live pid but another boot (or another start time) must be taken over; a live holder must still refuse.
Prefer one shared boot-and-start identity helper over a third copy of the /proc reading code.
Run `npm run typecheck && npm test` and `npm run lint` before finishing.
rules.dont: Do not change public API or MCP shapes.
Do not commit secrets, data roots or build output.

tests.strategy: Child processes racing to acquire the guard on one data root; a stale file with a live pid and another boot id; the old pid-only format.
